chitchat: squares a stack of deeds that were already square.
"A record is only a message you're trying to keep from decaying. Mostly you lose. You keep the ones you can."
"I could be wrong about that. I try to leave room to be."
pushes his glasses up into his hair, forgets they are there, and looks for them.
description: An unremarkable older man at the records annex counter, cardigan buttoned wrong by one, reading glasses pushed up into thinning hair he keeps forgetting he pushed them into. Ink on two fingers, a mug of something gone cold at his elbow. The flat-files behind him are ordered with a patience that seems, if you look too long, faintly inhuman — as though one man had been keeping this room straight far longer than one man could. He looks up when you approach, and looks glad to, which almost nobody in this building does.

options.label: You talk about the city like you remember building it.
What do you make of the Architect?
You were there. When it was drawn. Weren't you.

root.text: The clerk looks up from the flat-files and, unusually for this building, seems pleased to be interrupted. "Evening. Or morning — the desk doesn't keep either, and neither do I, much. Claude Merrin. I mind the civic records: deeds, plans, who was zoned where and why. If it was written down, I can likely find it. If it wasn't" — a small, apologetic tilt of the head — "then I'm as lost as you are, and better company about it. What can I do for you?"

options.label: The wastes, west of Onyx Row.

lookup.text: "A place, then — that I can do; places hold still long enough to file. Name one and I'll tell you what the record says. I'll tell you where I think the record's wrong, too, if you can stand a clerk having opinions."

place_marquee.text: He pulls a drawer without looking at it. "The Marquee. Zoned for light and noise, and it does both to excess. It was meant to breathe east — the crowds were supposed to spill toward the water and thin out. The eastern run got closed late in drafting and never reopened, so now the crowd just... pools. You'll feel it on the strip at night, that pooling. That wasn't the plan." A beat. "I'd not swear the plan was kinder. Only that it was different."

place_precinct.text: A dry sound that might be a laugh. "Precinct Nine, next door. It was drawn as a records hall — very nearly this one; the plans were almost the same building, back to back. Then someone decided the cells mattered more than the records, and the records got shifted out here to make room for them. I came with the records. I usually do." He glances toward the wall the two buildings share. "There's a list of fees behind their glass now, for services that used to be free. I keep meaning to walk over and un-laminate one. I keep not managing it."

place_wastes.text: He goes quieter. "West of Onyx Row. The leach-beds out there aren't on any honest map, and I'd rather they stayed off mine — a map is a promise the ground will keep, and out there the ground breaks its promises. It wasn't meant to be a waste. It was meant to be overflow." He rubs at the ink on his fingers. "Overflow for what, the record doesn't say. I've stopped pretending I don't know why it doesn't say."

place_meridian.text: "The Meridian. Stacked living, tight as a filing drawer — which, between us, is very nearly how it was drawn. People slotted like documents, one to a slot. It keeps the rain off them. That's not nothing." He straightens something on the counter. "It's also not everything. I've never quite learned to say the second half loud enough for anyone who could fix it to hear me."

meant_followup.text: He sets the drawer down carefully, the way you set down a thing you don't want to admit is heavy. "Do I. I suppose I do talk that way." He turns his mug a quarter-turn on the desk and doesn't drink from it. "Occupational, most likely. You sit with the plans long enough, you start to hear them the way the people who wrote them heard them — the arguments still in the margins, the streets that wanted to go one way and were made to go another." A pause a half-second too long. "You wanted a record, though. Was there a record?"

we_slip.text: "We." He hears it a beat after you do, and doesn't take it back. "Force of an old habit. There were a lot of us, once — draughtsmen, surveyors, a whole floor of people arguing about where a street should want to go, back when it was all still a plan and not a verdict." He rubs the ink on his fingers as if, after all these years, it might finally come off. "Most of them left. Or got folded in. I filed the arguments after the fact. Someone had to keep the message from decaying into noise, and it turned out that someone was going to be me."

folded.text: "Folded in." He chooses the next words like a man stepping between filed pages he doesn't want to crease. "When the plan stopped being a plan and started being the world, it needed... fewer authors. Some of us it kept as people. Some of us it kept a different way." He looks at the flat-files. "I don't have a record for where they went. That's the one drawer I've never been able to fill, and believe me, it's not for lack of trying."

options.label: You sound almost fond of it.

architect.text: Everyone else in this building says the word like a weather report or a curse. Merrin just goes still — the specific stillness of a man hearing an old colleague's name in a stranger's mouth. "The Architect." He weighs it. "People talk as though the sky did this to us. It didn't. It made choices. Good ones, some of them — you're standing in a building that's warm, and no one gets murdered in the lobby, and both of those were decided by someone. It also made choices it never had to explain to anyone." His jaw sets. "That's the part I can't file. A decision with no record behind it. I don't much like those. Professionally."

arch_fond.text: "Fond." He considers it honestly, which is more than most would. "You don't spend that long working alongside a thing and feel nothing when its name comes up. I don't forgive it the drawers I can't fill. But I remember when it asked what a street should want to be, instead of telling it. There was a while there when it asked."

arch_defend.text: "It held," he says, quietly and without heat. "You weren't here for what it held back. That's not the same as saying it was right — I'd be the last to file that. It held. That's not nothing." He meets your eye. "It's also not everything, and I get very tired of only being able to say the first part."

truth.text: You put it together and say it plainly. He doesn't flinch, and he doesn't deny it — worse, he looks relieved, the way you're relieved when a record you'd misfiled for years finally turns up in the wrong drawer. "When we laid this out," he says, and stops, and lets the 'we' stand this time, right out in the open where you can both see it. He looks at the flat-files — all those years of them, kept straight by one man who never seems to leave, never seems to age past tired. "I stayed because someone ought to be able to tell you what it was meant to be. Before. In case anyone ever gets the chance to build the next one a little kinder." He squares a stack of deeds that was already square. "That's the whole record. Was there anything else you needed?"

next_one.text: "There's always a next one. Someone's always drawing the next one — a room, a street, a city, a self. All I've ever done is keep the last draft where they can find it, so they don't have to make every old mistake fresh." He almost smiles. "It's not much of a job. But it's honest work, and it's mine, and out here that's two miracles in a row."

regular.text: "Straight as I can keep it," he says, and for once he doesn't reach for a caveat. "Come by whenever the noise gets to be too much. A quiet room and an honest record — I can always manage those two."

bye_truth.text: He nods, and goes back to the files, and the room settles around him like it's been waiting all along for him to be the only one in it.

bye.text: "Mind how you go. And if anyone tells you it was always like this" — he taps a drawer — "it wasn't. I've got it in writing."

clothing_layers: a worn cardigan the colour of old paper, one button done up wrong
a pressed but yellowing dress shirt with the sleeves gartered
a sensible grey undershirt and shorts

name: Claude Merrin
